title: Ash-e Reshteh
subtitle: Persian noodle and pulse soup
excerpt: A thick, hearty Persian soup of noodles, lentils, chickpeas, and spinach, finished with a spoonful of tangy kashk or thick yoghurt. Eaten for good luck at the Persian New Year, it is a meal in itself.
sourceNotes: Ash-e reshteh is one of Iran's most beloved soups. It is eaten at Nowruz and on special occasions. The noodles represent the threads of fate and are said to bring luck for the year ahead.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze without the kashk topping. Add fresh yoghurt when reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and freeze half.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Tastes better the next day. Thin with a little water when reheating.

content.text: The soup is very thick, more like a stew than a broth. Add water or stock if it becomes too stiff. The fried onion topping is not optional -- it adds the key finishing flavour.

items.prepNote: 1 diced for the soup, 1 finely sliced for the topping
use reshteh noodles -- or use linguine broken into short lengths
use kashk (fermented whey) if available -- otherwise thick yoghurt

content.text: Fry the diced onion in oil in a large pot for 8 minutes until golden. Add the turmeric and cinnamon. Stir for 1 minute.
Add the leek and cook for 5 minutes.
Add the lentils and stock. Bring to a boil. Simmer for 20 minutes.
Add the chickpeas, spinach, and noodles. Simmer for 15 more minutes until everything is soft and the soup is thick.
While the soup cooks, fry the sliced onion in oil over medium heat for 15 to 20 minutes until very dark and crispy. Set aside.
Season the soup with salt. Ladle into bowls.
Top with a generous spoonful of kashk or yoghurt and a pile of crispy fried onion.

items.symptom: Soup is too thick and stodgy
items.fix: Add more hot stock or water and stir. Ash-e reshteh thickens further as it stands -- always have extra stock ready.

items.symptom: Noodles have broken down into mush
items.cause: Cooked too long or added too early
items.fix: Add the noodles in the last 15 minutes only. Reshteh noodles soften quickly.

items.symptom: Kashk topping curdles when added to hot soup
items.fix: Spoon the kashk on top just before serving, not stirred in. The contrast of cold and hot is part of the dish.

content.text: Ash-e reshteh is eaten across Iran and has deep ritual significance. The noodles are said to represent the threads of fate and the direction life may take. It is eaten at Nowruz, the Persian New Year, to bring good fortune. It is also a common home comfort food in winter. The sharp tang of kashk and the sweet crunch of fried onion make it hard to stop eating.
